481	he fears gentiles. What does it mean, he fears gentiles?
482	Among the Persians there was
483	a day, their festival, when they worshipped fire, and on that day
484	no one was allowed to light a fire, except in the house of
485	their worship. So he is afraid they will see, so he
486	lit the Shabbat candle and wants to put it out.
487	Or because of bandits: he fears they will discover him.
488	He knows there are thieves here and he is afraid that
489	thieves, murderers, will discover him.
490	The third possibility is because of an evil spirit. HaShem
491	protect us, there is a person who is ill, mentally ill,
492	and he has fears. So now, when he sees
493	nothing, he is less afraid. When he sees, then
494	he gets worked up. So, because of an evil spirit. And if
495	for the sake of the sick person who is sleeping, in all these cases he
496	is exempt. Now we need to examine whether this speaks of a sick person
497	in danger or not in danger. Rabbenu
498	Ovadiah of Bartenura says it surely speaks of one in danger,
499	for if there is no danger, how is it permitted to put out a lamp?
500	So what is it? It speaks of a sick person in danger. Then
501	why "exempt"? It should say "permitted." The Rav says,
502	true, it really should say "permitted." Only because
503	the latter clause says "liable," here they wrote "exempt."
504	But in truth it is permitted. This is a matter of saving a life.
505	But if he puts it out to spare the lamp, to spare the oil, to spare
506	the wick, he is liable. Why? Because then he is not doing
507	it because of…
508	So he is doing it because of…
509	no reason, just stinginess like this, so it is forbidden
510	on Shabbat to extinguish. Although it is only rabbinic,
511	since regarding extinguishing, he is liable by Torah law
512	only if he did it for the sake of the wick. So it is only
513	rabbinic here, a melachah not needed for its own sake. Fine, but it is forbidden.
514	Rabbenu Ovadiah of Bartenura says: "to spare the wick"
515	and even though he does not need the extinguishing itself, but
516	for another purpose, so the wick will not burn or so the
517	lamp will not burst, still he is liable. Why? Because this Mishnah holds that
518	one is liable for a melachah not needed for its own sake.
519	Although we rule as halachah that
520	a melachah not needed for its own sake is exempt, here the Mishnah holds
521	that he is liable.
522	that he is liable.
523	Rabbi Yose exempts in every case except the wick, because
524	he makes charcoal.
525	Yes. Why does it say here "to spare the lamp, to spare the
526	oil, to spare the wick"? Is he really
527	sparing? The commentators say
528	that it is written in the Gemara, tractate Beitzah: all of a person's
529	sustenance is fixed for him from Erev Shabbat, sorry,
530	from Rosh HaShanah to Rosh HaShanah, except for the expenses of Shabbat
531	and Yom Tov, the expenses of his sons, and Torah study. It follows,
532	then, that
533	it follows, then, that when a person spares the lamp, spares
534	the wick, it only seems to him that he is sparing. The truth is
535	that it is not at his expense, because it is not at all
536	your account. It is an open check
537	from Above.
538	It only seems to you that you are sparing. "To spare the lamp, to spare
539	the oil, to spare the wick": the law is that he is liable.
540	Mishnah 6: For three transgressions women die in the hour of
541	their childbirth. The hour of childbirth is a time of danger, and when a person is
542	in a time of danger, they judge him. So they come and tell us
543	there are three mitzvot that depend on the woman, that are placed upon
544	the woman, and so when a woman, Heaven forbid, does not
545	keep them properly, then at a time of danger such as childbirth
546	they judge her for them. What are they? For not being careful
547	with niddah, with challah, and with lighting the candle. These three mitzvot
548	depend on the woman in every Jewish home. Among
549	the Mizrachi communities, the custom is that before the wedding they hold
550	a party called the henna. What is henna? An acronym:
551	Challah, Niddah, Hadlakat haNer, lighting the candle, because these are the mitzvot
552	placed on every Jewish woman in her home. These are
553	mitzvot belonging to the Jewish woman, and when a Jewish woman
554	is about to marry, they make her a henna. What is henna?
555	Challah, Niddah, lighting the candle.
556	The last Mishnah of this chapter: Three things
557	a person must say in his house on Erev Shabbat at twilight:
558	Have you tithed? Have you made the eruv? Light the candle.
559	On Erev Shabbat at twilight, and not earlier, because if he
560	says it earlier, at noon, they will say, "We'll do it later, later," and they will forget. But when it is already
561	close to dark, "Have you tithed?"
562	close to dark, "Have you tithed?"
563	Now it is urgent. "Have you made the eruv of boundaries
564	and the eruv of courtyards? And light the candle."
565	Why does it not say "Have you lit the candle"? You are blind?
566	You can see they have not lit it, so say "Light!"
567	Now, if it is doubtful whether it is dark or not dark. What does "doubtful
568	whether it is dark" mean? It means one star is not yet
569	night. Three stars is already night. Two
570	stars is called a doubtful dusk, doubtful whether it is dark.
571	One does not tithe what is certainly untithed. Why? It is a rabbinic decree,
572	because of the repair of the produce. And one does not immerse the utensils
573	for the same reason. This is called the repair of a vessel. And one does not
574	light the candles. This is already truly Torah law.
575	But one does tithe demai, because most of the people
576	tithe, and only because we are concerned do we
577	tithe, so this can still be done in such a situation.
578	And one makes the eruv of courtyards, because this too
579	is
580	only a stringency, since King Solomon instituted it, but
581	this
582	can still be done. And one may insulate the cholent,
583	meaning it is permitted to insulate the hot food, but of course not
584	with something that adds heat. With something that adds heat, even
585	from Erev Shabbat, it is forbidden, forbidden to insulate. Here
586	it speaks of something that does not add heat. So
587	this is still permitted to do. And so far the Mishnah, tractate
588	Shabbat, chapter 2, for today.

591	why is the law that it is forbidden to light with lamps whose oil
592	has a bad smell? The answer is, Rabbah says:
593	because its smell is bad, it is a decree lest he leave it and go out.
